The twelve-point-eight per cent figure this round was briefed on does not reproduce — the control arm measures twenty-eight to thirty-five, and the file's own earlier note agrees, so the number that justified the round was another unlocalised measurement. The hemisphere fill everyone has been arguing about for five rounds is eight hundredths of one per cent of the deck's light and has nothing to give. And every shadow setting in the environment file is dead code, overwritten every frame by the render pipeline; a sweep across bias, radius, map size and intensity returned byte-identical frames.

What shipped: the overdrive rescue, which took the money shot from eight times darker than the darkest reference to sitting below the ordinary-frame median and above both references that are themselves supers, with its colour back. The wash near-field, replacing a falloff with zero derivative at the tube — a plateau exactly where a real lamp is steepest — and buying thirty-seven per cent more modulation in the air above the strip. And a wall-falloff gate anchored to thirteen thousand fixed world points rather than a pixel rectangle, which holds to eleven per cent across seven framings where the old one swung fifty-seven. The old gate was reading a sign plate.

log.title: The body was rigid, and the frame archive never existed
paras: Animation 67, lighting 78, interface 74, stage 73, character 69, impact 66. The first dedicated animation round since round twenty, and the largest move that axis has ever made — which is an indictment, because four consecutive rounds went to lighting while the worst axis in the project sat untouched and drifted down two points.

The finding is that the body had no kinetic chain. The rubric's own text for a ninety-plus score is that the hips lead and the head lags — a strike drives from the floor up. That is a claim about ordering, and ordering is measurable. Driven through the offline rig sampler across all thirty-four clips that declare an impact: median hips-to-tip lag, zero ticks. Median chain concordance, 0.50 — pure chance. Median hip speed on the contact frame, as a fraction of the hips' own peak, 1.00. Nine clips peaked every link — hips, both spine joints, chest, shoulder, elbow, wrist — on a single tick. The pelvis was at its own top speed on the exact frame the fist landed, which is the opposite of how a strike transfers momentum.

The cause was localised in the data rather than guessed at. Round eleven re-keyed the drive one key per tick on a ramp whose exponent is solved per span so that a fixed fraction of the travel always lands on the contact tick — solved per span and applied to every driving bone, so they all arrive together. It bought the contact-frame speed it was written for and flattened the chain doing it. And the operator already in the file structurally could not repair it: its taper is zero at the pivot, so it can separate two bones during the startup and never at contact, for any strength.

The new operator advances the proximal chain and holds the authored contact value, so the contact pose is unchanged by construction — verified at zero bones drifted, to six decimal places, across all ninety-two clips, with no move's startup, active or recovery frames touched. Concordance went to 0.74, lag to four ticks, hip speed at contact to zero, and the number of clips whose chain ran backwards from seventeen to two.

Then the critics found something that invalidates a great deal of this project's own history. The ignore rule was the single word shots, which matches the dossier's screenshot directory as well as the working one. Not one capture from any round survives in git. The question every axis keeps raising — did this fall because the work got worse, or because the frame it is scored on changed — has been unanswerable by construction for twenty-eight rounds, and would have stayed that way. It is fixed, the archive is tracked, and it now records its own revision, commit and resolution.

The archive was also the wrong resolution, and that faked a catastrophe. It held 1280 by 720 frames while captures deliver 1920 by 1080. Compared naively on identical crop coordinates, the stage critic's nine floor crops read between fifty-six and eighty-five per cent down — the floor detail apparently destroyed. Scale-matched, the same crops read plus five point seven, plus one point three, and zero. A critic quoting the first table would have led with a disaster that does not exist, and the impact critic hit the same trap from the other side, with a pixel region landing on background and reporting that the effect had vanished entirely.

Two things were reverted under the charter rule that a change measuring worse ships the measurement instead of the feature. The fine particle population regressed the very metric it was built to raise — discrete component count down on all three impact frames, the fine end worst at minus forty-seven per cent on the flagship — and the critic controlled for the resolution trap by round-tripping through 720p, finding the resampler's bias runs the same direction, so the true drop is larger than quoted. And one clip's chain budget was disabled: its acceleration reversed twelve times along the approach where it had reversed twice, because the gate set governing the new operator never included approach smoothness. It bought chain ordering by spending precisely what the rubric penalises as linear interpolation.

Two admissions. The particle gate I forwarded into the briefing — count eleven-to-twenty-nine rising to thirty-five-to-one-hundred-fifty-two — had no measurement script, no defined region, and its before-figure does not reproduce under any mask anyone could construct; the same baseline measures one hundred and six to two hundred and six. Re-deriving numbers before passing them on is rule four of my own preamble, written three rounds ago. And I cited an evidence shot that has never existed in the capture list at all, which the manifest cannot catch, because completeness is validated against the list itself rather than against a declared roster.

The animation axis is scored on one clip out of ninety-two. Every evidence frame in the project photographs the same uppercut, and that clip received the smallest fix in the file — a reduced two-bone chain on a half-tick budget. Ninety-two clips diagnosed, twenty-eight improved, and the round's median gain is invisible in all four scored frames. That is a harness limit, not an art limit, and it is the first thing the next round has to fix.

log.title: The instruments were lying, and the game could not be played on a phone
paras: Lighting 78, interface 74, stage 73, character 69, impact 67, animation 66. Round 29 moved nothing and was worth more than several rounds that did, because four critics independently established that a great deal of what this project has measured was measured wrongly.

Twenty of twenty-five scored frames were rendered below native and compared against native references. Eight distinct render scales across one pass, from 0.72 to 1.00, with the adaptive controller live on seventeen of eighteen shots — one arena rendered at 1382 by 777 and written out as 1920 by 1080 by the screenshot, then judged beside a Tekken press capture. Because the controller was live, the scale was set by whatever the machine's frame timing happened to be, so it was not even reproducible between two runs of the same build. The cause was mine: a round-26 change that handed renderer settings back after a frozen shot, made to stop one shot corrupting the frame-rate probe. It protected the performance instrument and silently degraded the evidence instrument for every other frame, with nothing watching the second. Every shot now renders at native with the controller off.

The kinetic-chain metric awarded its maximum score to the exact failure it existed to catch. Its ordering test accepted equality, so two links peaking on the same tick counted as correctly ordered — meaning a body whose every joint fires simultaneously, the purest possible robotic motion, scored a flawless one. Verified on the straight punch: perfect under the old rule with all ten pairs tied, zero under a strict one. Across two hundred and eleven moves the tie rule reads a median of 0.70 where strict reads 0.10. Essentially the whole of the previous round's apparent improvement lived in the tie. And that round's headline — median lag zero rising to four ticks — does not reproduce; the true median is zero and four is near the maximum. A maximum reported as a median, the fourth consecutive round launched on a figure that did not survive re-derivation.

The frame archive had been fixed twice and had taken neither time. The ignore rule was corrected, but the archive was still exported by hand afterwards, so it drifted to certifying a commit ninety minutes older than the frames beside it, holding eighteen shots where the run had twenty-five, and recording every frame at the size it was written rather than the size it was rendered. A hand-exported archive drifts by construction. It is now written by the capture run itself, with the commit read from git rather than declared, and a flag marking whether the tree was dirty.

The impact gate was measuring armour. Its definition of an effect pixel scored a precision of 0.019 to 0.375 against a per-pixel ground truth built by rendering the same frozen frame with the effects visible and hidden — five pixels in eight it counted were not effects, and it missed four fifths of what was. The mask was landing on a white robot's plates, panel speculars and the damage badge. The previous round's number did not reproduce; this one reproduces exactly and measures the wrong object, which is worse. Every figure the axis carried is withdrawn, including the deltas that justified reverting a change which may simply have been noise.

Then the player reported bugs, and they were worse than they sounded. Three quarters of the airborne moveset did not exist: the requirement flag appeared on exactly two moves in the entire game, both bound to right kick, so jumping and pressing anything else did nothing. Ducking and pressing right kick matched a move that could never fire on the ground. Overdrive on mobile was a notation bug — the move was authored as a quarter-circle plus a button, so a tap on the pad sent the button with no motion and could never match.

And an audit of mine was wrong in the most instructive way. I reported the state and button matrix as twelve of twelve on every archetype, having driven the matcher with a hand-built buffer. A synthesised buffer cannot contain the defect, because the defect is created upstream in the history the real input path writes: a held direction wrote itself into that history twice, so the motion test read a double-tap nobody entered. Holding down and pressing right punch produced an eighty-six frame unblockable instead of a poke, and holding back turned every back move into a dash — which is precisely why back and right punch were reported as broken while my test showed them resolving perfectly. Testing the matcher is not testing the game.

Throws had the same shape: three existed, and none could be pressed, because a chord required both buttons inside the same sixteen milliseconds. On a handset they were unreachable entirely, since any two-finger tap was swallowed as an overdrive before the buttons could be read — an entire mechanic absent on the platform most people play on. A rejected grab also paid out through the strike path as guaranteed unblockable damage during a juggle.

What shipped: ten robot-specific finishers, one per machine, each with a condition stated in words on screen because an input the player cannot trigger reads as broken. Thirty-one signature moves that make two robots sharing an archetype stop being the same fighter. A move list reachable from pause and character select, verified at four viewports down to a 390-pixel handset. And a menu button on the touch HUD, because until now a phone player who started a match could not leave it.

log.title: Six rounds of advice measured brightness and called it detail
paras: Impact 72, lighting 78, interface 74, stage 74, character 69, animation 66. The impact move is five points, the largest single-axis gain this project has recorded, and it is the first one measured by an instrument nobody has since found a hole in — the effects gate rebuilt in round 30, which renders each frozen contact frame twice, once with the effect meshes visible and once hidden, so the difference is the effect itself rather than a guess about which pixels are bright enough to count.

The round existed because I found my own blocker. For six rounds every brief I wrote forbade new geometry on the grounds that the triangle budget was forty-six per cent over its ceiling. The charter says the opposite in bold, in the same section that number lives in: frames are bought by shading fewer pixels or fewer lights, not by fewer draws and not by fewer triangles. The nine hundred thousand figure is a compliance metric sitting beside the draw-call budget, which the same paragraph measures at 1.2 microseconds per call and explicitly calls a compliance metric rather than a performance one. I had treated it as a hard ceiling without checking what it measured, and in doing so blocked the single most repeated recommendation in the project.

So the round unblocked it and spent geometry on authored hero clusters — and then disproved the reason for doing so. The agent built the instrument the gate named and swept forty-eight definition variants looking for one that reproduced the brief. None did. Our dead-tile fraction is thirty-one, forty-six and forty per cent under the definition that reproduces the reference's forty-one point seven exactly; the briefed figure was five to nineteen. The skydeck is emptier than the reference it was being unfavourably compared to. The claim that a reference had lower median tile contrast than any of our shots is backwards. The two halves of the headline comparison had been computed under different definitions, which is how a comparable number came to look like a fivefold deficit.

And the metric was not a detail metric at all. Absolute tile contrast is linear in image brightness. One reference has exactly the same peakedness as our frames and a seventy per cent higher peak purely from being two and a half times brighter; another is less peaked than every one of our frames while carrying the highest peak in the set. On the exposure-invariant statistic we were already inside the reference band on concentration. The gap is level, not distribution — and the target I set exceeded all three matched references in linear light, so it was unreachable by construction. Six rounds of critic advice, one round of work, and the finding is that the advice measured brightness and called it detail.

The hero clusters are therefore out. They cost about a millisecond and four frames a second at the full pass, for a gate that was not met and a theory that was disproved. That is the charter's own rule — an agent that measures its own change made things worse ships the measurement instead of the feature — applied to a round I designed and argued for. The geometry unblock was still correct; what I unblocked it for was not the real gap.

The harder finding is that the game is not at sixty frames a second and I had been reporting that it was. Three repeated measurements of an unchanged tree land at 58.5, 58.5 and 58.8. The 60.2 I had been quoting was real but it was the lucky end of a noisy distribution, and I read single figures instead of repeating them — which is the exact discipline I have spent this project imposing on everyone else. The charter constraint has been missed for some time.

The next round has one job, and the charter names it in the same bold sentence I misread six rounds ago. Frames are bought by shading fewer pixels or fewer lights. The frame is roughly eighteen milliseconds proportional to shaded pixels and eleven fixed, with an arena covering eighty-five per cent of the screen through several overdraw layers and fifteen analytic lights. That is where the missing millisecond and a half has to come from.

log.title: Six instruments failed, three counters worked, and the frame came back 0.45 milliseconds
paras: Two rounds spent on the one hard constraint the charter states outright: sixty frames a second at 1080p. The game was missing it. It is still missing it, by 0.13 milliseconds, in one arena at one camera — and meeting it everywhere else. Before these rounds the miss was 0.58.

Almost none of that time went on rendering. It went on discovering that this project could not measure itself, and then building instruments that can. Six timing instruments failed. Wall clock in separate windows read a null arm at 18, 40 and 62 milliseconds. Paired blocks drifted 37 to 55 between arms. GPU timer queries reported 223 milliseconds of work inside an 84 millisecond frame — monotone in fill, but uncalibrated by a factor nobody could pin down. Amplification, which raises the signal by drawing a surface sixteen times, raises the noise with it, because contention scales with frame time. Each of those announced itself with an impossible number: negative costs, effects larger than the frame.

The last two did not announce themselves, and they are the ones worth remembering. A probe measuring repeated blocks off a single match start watched its median fall from 16.9 to 11.8 milliseconds — a clean, monotone, entirely fictional gain, because by the seventh block it was timing a knockout cinematic rather than a fight. And a quiet-gate that waited for the machine to clear matched its own wrapper shell in the process list, so it waited fifteen minutes for a machine that was already free. One manufactures a result, the other manufactures an obstacle, and both look like the system working correctly while you watch.

What did work were counters rather than stopwatches. A fragment counter that renders each layer alone against a real depth buffer and sums the pixels it writes. A coverage counter. A pixel-identity check. All three are bit-reproducible and completely immune to a busy machine — two runs at two framings agreed to half a per cent while six foreign browsers competed for the GPU. The rule that falls out of it is short: where a question can be answered by counting, do not time it.

Those counters immediately retracted a premise this project had been steering by for five rounds. A volumetric mote sheet had been described as covering forty per cent of the screen at four layers deep. Measured, it is three hundred and fifty-seven fragments — three and a half orders of magnitude smaller, and impossible beforehand, since the shader caps every mote at eleven pixels square. The false belief came from a raycast: Three's raycaster tests points against a one-metre distance threshold that has nothing whatever to do with their rendered footprint. A raycast is not a render.

The same counters found something no stopwatch and no screenshot could: three of the arena's five authored light shafts draw nothing at all. Two sit behind the back wall, one is off the left edge. Sixty per cent of the venue's volumetric lighting is tinted, breathed and updated every frame and retires zero pixels — and the quality ladder that thins the shafts on lower tiers removes the only two visible ones last, so a tier drop takes away all remaining atmosphere before it takes away anything invisible.

The frames that were recovered came from two shader folds, and both were defended without a clock. One material bound the same texture to three separate samplers, so every shaded pixel fetched one texel three times; another read a wetness mask out of a texture the normal-map chunk had already sampled at the same coordinate one line earlier. Ten texture units became eight; thirteen became twelve. Both verified by pixel identity — nought differing pixels out of two million, against a positive control that moves a million — on materials this project had already documented as sitting at the sixteen-sampler hardware limit.

The honest close is that the per-file split of that 0.45 milliseconds is not established. A replication found the baseline itself drifting by 0.25 milliseconds between sessions, which is exactly the size of the effects being attributed to individual files. Totals survive that; splits do not. Before dividing a measured total among causes, the drift between measurements has to be smaller than the pieces — and this project has now been caught by that same shape three times.

Nothing about how the game looks changed in either round, and a frozen-frame instrument with the camera pinned to literal coordinates proves it: the difference between the tree before and after sits at or below the difference between two captures of the same build, measured against a control that sees the key light at four to nine times the noise.

log.title: Re-scored on repaired instruments, and every axis went down
paras: Lighting 72, impact 71, interface 71, stage 67, character 66, animation 58. Average 72.8 to 67.5. Six axes, six declines, and not one of them is a regression in the game.

Every score this project had was produced by tooling that has since been shown defective. Twenty of twenty-five frames were rendering below native and being compared against native press captures, at a scale set by machine load and not reproducible between runs. The animation metric awarded its maximum to the exact failure it existed to catch, because its ordering test counted a tie as correct — so a body whose every joint fires on one tick scored perfect. The effects gate was landing on a white robot's armour plates at between two and thirty-seven per cent precision, and was blind to five of the eight systems it claimed to measure. The frame archive was untracked, then stale, then at the wrong resolution. Two certified frames contained no three-dimensional scene at all and passed every gate. All of that is now repaired, and this round is the first score taken through instruments that hold up.

Each of the six critics was asked, as a required field, whether its number is comparable to its predecessor. All six answered no, unprompted and for six different reasons. That is the round's real result: the old numbers were not slightly generous, they were measuring something else.

The animation drop is the largest and the least alarming. That axis was judged for thirty rounds on a single clip out of ninety-two — every evidence frame in the project photographed the same uppercut, and that clip is one of the better ones in the library. This round was the first with a roundhouse, a straight, a launch reaction and a locomotion cycle on screen. The score fell because the sample widened, not because the work got worse. The sharpest line in the round is the critic's own blind description of a crop it did not yet know was ours: standing, both feet flat and parallel, knees near-straight, torso vertical. That is the contact frame of the straight punch.

Character rendering should have gone up and did not. Both of the old biases — sub-native rendering and a smaller archive — push the same way, toward softer and worse, so a like-for-like re-score at full resolution ought to have beaten the old number. It came in lower for a reason the old instrument could not see at all. Lighting is stranger still: it won its blind comparison against the reference, and still scored down six points, on the axis the capture defect distorted least. Its critic could not credit the repair and instead found that the measurements the previous grade decisions rested on do not re-derive.

Two findings arrived that no amount of tuning would have produced. The comparable-reference subset handed to critics for several rounds includes a frame whose stage is entirely hidden behind a full-screen effect — the stage axis has been partly benchmarking against an image with no visible stage in it. And the interface's typeface does not exist: the stylesheet names three faces, none of which ship on this platform, with no font registered anywhere in the codebase, so the entire interface renders in a fallback on every machine and in the intended face on none. That also breaks the charter's own rule that everything ships generated in code.

None of this says the previous thirty-three rounds were wasted. The game demonstrably improved and many of those rounds fixed real defects with real evidence. It says something narrower and more uncomfortable: a scoring loop is only as good as its instruments, and this one spent thirty-three rounds tuning against numbers that were systematically kind to it. Sixty-seven and a half is the first average worth building on.

log.title: We had the axis the camera cannot see, and none of the axes it can
paras: Interface 76, lighting 72, impact 71, stage 64, character 66, animation 60. Interface gained five, the best single-axis move in many rounds; animation two; stage lost three, and that loss is a re-pricing rather than a regression.

The interface's typeface did not exist. Counted on this machine: Eurostile Extended zero, Bank Gothic zero, Segoe UI Semibold zero, Arial Narrow four. And it was worse than reported — the label stack names the same three absent families in a different order, so the design's two distinct faces had been one face all along. It is now three families compiled to real TrueType at boot and registered through the font API: eight cuts, a hundred and twelve glyphs each, a hundred kilobytes, twelve milliseconds once at startup, no network and no borrowed outlines.

That face shipped rejected the first time. Every one of the eight cuts was refused by the browser over a single seed in one loop, so every element fell back to the system stack — precisely the bug the generated face existed to fix. Nothing in the project could have caught it: the checker imports the typeface through a shim where the font API does not exist, so the installer takes its no-op path and the font was never parsed by anything until it reached a browser. A generated asset with no validator that runs where it is built. The checker now compiles all eight cuts offline and validates them, and that guard was tested by putting the bug back and watching it fail sixteen times before it was trusted.

The animation result is the most useful thing in the round because it half-falsified the brief I wrote. I predicted the library's contrapposto angles were near zero. For twist that is false — the stance blades the pelvis twenty-eight degrees and counter-rotates the spine nineteen, giving a median of eighteen degrees of hip-to-shoulder separation, squarely inside the reference band the critic itself quoted. It is true for every axis in the frontal plane: pelvis level to half a degree, shoulder line parallel to it within one, spine straight to three millimetres over its whole span. In other words the library already had the axis a side-on fight camera cannot resolve, and none of the axes it can.

A second finding nobody asked for: twenty-eight of thirty-four attacks lose what separation they have at the moment of contact. The straight punch goes from eighteen degrees to eight. The critic had described that exact frame, blind, as shoulders parallel to hips — and it is, but only there.

The fix is a solved pose delta rather than ninety-two hand edits: the pelvis rolls eight degrees and the compensation is solved numerically against the rig's own kinematics so that both ankles and both toes land at zero displacement and the chest keeps its world position, which is what keeps the arms, neck and head where the animator put them. Seventy-seven of ninety-two clips took it, no clip changed duration or contact tick, and the worst movement of any striking anchor is one millimetre. It is honestly short: the thirteen kicks took nothing and the attacks took almost nothing, so the contact frames a critic actually picks references out of are barely touched. The named next step is re-solving that compensation per keyframe with the two-bone solver the animator already carries.

Stage fell three points without anything getting worse. The panel caught a screen-space light band on the rooftop and fourteen unlit black quads sitting in the cistern's reflective floor, and both are present, byte for byte, in the previous round's capture. They are newly counted, not newly broken — the earlier sixty-seven was pricing an arena set that contained them.

The dead light shafts were repositioned and the fix landed, verified by an offline depth rasteriser rather than a stopwatch: three shafts that retired exactly zero fragments now retire two per cent each, total atmosphere fill up from twenty-three per cent of frame to thirty-six, at no measurable frame cost. And yet the critic found no new beam visible anywhere in the pit. Both are true. They exist now and they are still too faint to read as light. Existence was the fix; visibility is the next one.

That agent also corrected three numbers in the brief it was given and one in the project's own profiling notes — including a coverage split that cannot arise from mirror-image geometry at a centred camera, and a complaint about the quality ladder that was inverted: the ladder had been dropping only the invisible shafts, so it was cutting none of the cost.

log.title: The axis we optimised for two rounds points at the camera
paras: Interface 76, lighting 72, impact 71, stage 66, character 64, animation 62. Average 68.5. Two rounds of pose work were aimed at the wrong axis, and two independent parties found it in the same hour.

An outside model was brought in with shell access and no stake in this project's assumptions, told to edit nothing, and asked to assume at least three uncaught measurement errors existed. It found six. Separately, this round's animation agent reached the same central conclusion from the rig rather than from pixels. Both say the camera-plane reasoning was inverted.

Measured by projecting the posed rig through the fight camera itself: eight degrees at the hips buys about one degree of on-screen lean per degree of sagittal pitch, three tenths of a degree for yaw, and for roll — which is what the contrapposto operator writes — between minus seven and plus one, and approximately zero on the attack contact frames. The null reads exact zeros in all thirty-six cells. The camera sits at zero lateral offset, because its own framing code clamps that term to zero when the fighters are symmetric, so it looks straight down a fighter's left-right axis. Sagittal lean is what it resolves. The outside audit measured the same thing from pixels and got twenty-two pixels of displacement for lean against eight for roll and six for twist.

The spine told the same story and nobody had decomposed it. The bow measurement was taken on the model's X axis — which is the camera axis. Split into components, the in-screen curve is nineteen millimetres across ninety-two clips with an interquartile spread of one point two. The in-screen spine curve is a single constant inherited from the rest pose and not one clip varies it. That is precisely the critic's complaint about a straight column, and the operator shipped last round could never have moved it.

The fix named for this round turned out not to be implementable, and the reason is worth more than the fix. Re-solving the compensation per keyframe needs a shared key-time grid, and only five of ninety-two clips have one; the rest sit off-grid with fractional key times, and different bones disagree about the easing at the same tick. Resampling would mean linearising eased segments, and bisecting a snap misstates it by nearly a fifth of its range — around ten degrees mid-swing.

So the agent shipped something better instead: an operator that never touches the hips at all, which makes the legs, the feet, the root and every leg-compensation question disappear by construction. Fifty-six of ninety-two clips took it. The thirteen kicks the previous operator could not touch are the entire point — a kick's hitbox is on a foot, so the torso is free at the moment of contact — and eight of them now take the full delta at zero millimetres of anchor movement, verified against a positive control on the same code path where the hand moves up to twenty-seven centimetres. On-screen lean at the judged tick went from three degrees to twelve, and the number of clips standing within five degrees of vertical fell from fifty-five to eleven.

The audit's most valuable finding was not about animation at all. The character axis has been steered for four rounds by a comparison of our mean against the reference's seventy-fifth percentile. Re-derived here on a third instrument, our fight framings measure twenty and twenty-one against a reference pooled median of fourteen — they exceed it. Only the parked closeup sits below. There is no general detail deficit on that axis; there is one framing that reads below reference and two that read above, and the work was steered by the weakest of the three against an incomparable statistic.

And the performance constraint is measured at a resolution the charter does not name. The charter says sixty frames a second at 1920 by 1080. The probe measures at eighty-five per cent scale — 1632 by 918 — while the critics score frames at full resolution. At native the documented cost is closer to twenty-two milliseconds, which is forty-six frames a second, not fifty-nine and a half. Every performance claim in this project now needs two numbers.

The method lesson is the one to keep. Nine measurement errors were found by internal agents across thirty-six rounds; an outside model found six more in a single pass, two of which redirect the project. The difference is not capability. Every internal agent was briefed with the numbers it was meant to check, and inherited them as context rather than as claims. A measurement record needs auditing by something that was not briefed from it.

log.when: Round 37, the phone, and a second external audit
log.title: A player picked it up, and every instrument that mattered was pointing somewhere else
paras: The shipping tier now runs at seventy-one frames a second, up from fifty-nine. That number exists because the previous round measured at the wrong resolution: the probe was reading eighty-five per cent scale while the charter names 1920 by 1080, and at native the miss was five point four milliseconds rather than the thirteen hundredths of a millisecond the record claimed. Corrected, the round found five point four milliseconds to give back. Native itself is still about one point eight milliseconds short of sixty, and that gap is now stated in both numbers every time it is reported.

Between those measurements a person played it on a phone, and that was worth more than any of them. They asked three questions in a row. How do I leave training mode. How can I block on mobile. And, after switching tabs and coming back, why is it not full screen any more. The first two controls were both on the screen they were looking at: the menu button under the timer and the block pad at mid-left. The game was correct and the player could not tell, which is a different kind of defect from a bug and one no capture can photograph.

What shipped for them: the block pad and the menu button made opaque rather than ghosted, and fullscreen re-requested on any touch that finds the game windowed instead of only on the first one. Alongside those, the round closed the gaps a controller had hidden. All four limbs now answer while airborne and while crouching, back plus a punch or kick reaches its move, throws are a two-finger chord that no longer pays out as an unblockable strike, and every robot has a signature string and a finisher with a trigger condition, all of them readable from a move list that opens from the pause menu and from character select.

Then two outside models were asked to assume the measurement record was wrong, and between them found six more places where it was. The pattern across both audits is the finding. Not one of them was a bug in the game. Every one was a bug in what the project believed it was measuring, and in five of six cases the correction already existed in writing somewhere in the repo while the code or the briefs carried on using the old number.

The animation axis carried a fifteen-to-twenty degree reference band that appears in no measurement of any reference here and cannot: the references are single press stills with no rig, and absolute hip-to-shoulder yaw is not recoverable from one uncalibrated view. It is the same error as the character axis, retired the same way. The impact axis is worse than mismatched — the best image-only method for telling an effect pixel from an armour pixel reaches a quarter of the accuracy needed on the flagship reference, so closing a particle gap to Tekken cannot move that score, because the comparison cannot be made at all. And the stage frame list still named a reference that a discard list three lines above it had already rejected as having no floor in it, after the same conclusion had been written down twice elsewhere. A discard list the frame list does not honour is decoration. It is removed.

The last of the six was the highest-scoring axis. Interface is seventy-six, and it has missed every interface defect this project has shipped, because it grades the craft of the chrome already on screen from a still image, and a still image does not have a thumb. It scored seventy-six through a missing typeface, through a touch pad that ate character-select taps, through there being no way at all to leave a match on a phone, and through the player above finding neither control they needed.

So the axis now has an instrument that walks the path instead of photographing it. Touch only, no keyboard fallback, no reaching into the game to advance a screen; targets found by the text a player would read and checked for occlusion before they are tapped; start, inspect, lock, fight, menu, move list, close, leave, at two landscape phone sizes. It runs the path twice unchanged to prove the answer does not depend on the run, and once with the pause button hidden to prove it fails when a control cannot be found. If either control misbehaves it reports no verdict rather than a result.

On its first run the path passed, eight steps of eight, at both sizes. The game is operable by thumb from end to end, and that is worth saying plainly because the framing going in was pessimistic and the measurement disagreed. What it did find was three navigation buttons twenty-seven pixels tall. The button is sized in ems, the screen root collapses to its twelve-pixel floor on a short landscape viewport, and at the millimetre-per-pixel figure this project measured on a real handset that is four and a half millimetres — half an adult thumb. Two of the three were leave-the-match and open-the-move-list, which is to say the two the player could not use. They are now forty-four, the floor the touch code derives from its own measurements.

One more finding, and it is not a flattering one. The mobile audit opened by reporting that the two handset screenshots the brief called the ground truth were not on disk. They never were. The player pasted them into a conversation and nobody wrote them out, and the brief sent them to an outside model as the most important evidence in the task. That is the same failure as the discarded stage reference and the invented degree band, only cited to an agent instead of to the code, and caught in thirty seconds by the one party that had not been told to trust it.
